newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Biggest industry trade deal set for infotech.
newsitem.headline: Biggest industry trade deal set for infotech.

text.p: Up to 30 countries looked set on Thursday to scrap tariffs on $600 billion worth of information technology products in what officials called the biggest ever trade liberalisation deal for a single sector.

The deal, carved out in four days of talks at the inaugural World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting in Singapore, would remove tariffs on a wide range of high-technology products from fibre optic cables to computer monitors by 2000.

Drawn up by the European Union (EU) and the United States, the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) already has the support of 29 countries, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt told reporters.
"This is probably the biggest trade liberalisation agreement ever produced on a sectoral basis," Peter Carl, EU chief negotiator on the ITA, told a news conference.
Carl said he expected countries accounting for up to 85 percent of world trade in information technology goods to sign up by Friday.
European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan hailed the proposal as a huge step towards global free commerce.
"It will be good for the IT industry, and will act as a catalyst for industrial growth. As such it will be good for the whole world economy," Brittan said in a statement.
The Big Four trade powers -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- had set the pact as a key target to be able to declare this week's WTO a real success.

The deal would scrap tariffs on some 180 products in the fast-growing sector, including capacitors (energy-storing devices used in computers), digital photocopiers, fibre optics cables, computer monitors, telecommunications equipment, computer software and semiconductors.
"Almost every family is using equipment in the field of information technology," Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade Anneke van Dok told a news conference.
"Prices will come down because of the agreement we've just achieved," she said.
The final compromise excluded consumer electronics and audio materials.
Tariff cuts would take place in four stages, beginning in July 1997 and ending on January 1, 2000, at the latest, subject to some agreed exceptions.

In addition to the 15 members of the European Union, the countries signed up for ITA so far were Australia, Canada, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Iceland, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Norway, Philippines, Singapore, Switzerland, Turkey and the United States, Rexrodt said.
U.S. acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the benefits to world trade from the ITA would far exceed the financial savings from tariff reductions.

"The extent of tariff savings, which I guess would be quite hefty, doesn't begin to measure the ultimate economic benefits of agreements of this sort because of the more rapid growth in trade that tends to accompany tariff reductions," she told reporters.
Industry analysts said the pact could speed up the development of the global information technology sector, which was currently growing at around 15 percent per year.

EU officials said the final deal still depended on countries representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector joining the pact by March 15, 1997, but said they were sure that target would be met.
"The EU is already confident that by March 15 the 90 percent target is likely to be achieved," the EU said in a statement.
